newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU finance ministers set to tackle EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: EU finance ministers set to tackle EMU budget pact.

text.p: Hard bargaining over a disciplinary budget accord for countries joining a common European currency is expected to dominate a meeting of EU finance ministers on Monday.
The effort to secure a so-called budget stability pact has become one of the most difficult hurdles in nailing down a blueprint for economic and monetary union (EMU).

Coming at time of renewed debate over the Bundesbank's monetary stance and exchange rate policies between Paris and Bonn, the inclusion of a budget pact is seen as an integral part of a credible and sustainable monetary union.

Yet intrasigence by Germany over certain elements of the pact has left negotiations within the 15-nation bloc at a standstill, and most expect Monday's ministerial session to end with little progress.
Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said on Friday it was unclear whether he and his colleagues could resolve their differences over the budget pact's fine print.

"It is possible but not entirely certain," Asbrink said, adding the main obstacle was a definition of what constitutes "exceptional and temporary" economic circumstances -- in other words an unusually sharp economic downturn.
Under the proposed plan, countries running annual deficits above three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) could face stiff fines if they failed to curb expenditure.

But if a government could show that a severe recession was behind the deterioration of its public finances, it might be able to avoid sanctions. A quantitative expression of such a downturn is where the debate is centered.

Germany wants the recession defined as a two percent annual decline in GDP. Others have argued for a less rigid approach, preferring a range -- a fall in output of between 0.5 and 2.0 percent -- that would force EU finance ministers to decide whether fines were appropriate.
Financial markets have shown little worry over the slow pace of negotiations, with many taking a pragmatic view that an accord will eventually be agreed.
"I have the impression that so far markets understand that there are tough negotiations but they have no proof that it could lead to failure," said Eric Chaney, economist at Morgan Stanley in Paris.
Confidence that EMU will be launched as planned has remained steadfast even amid this week's heated exchange in France over the merits of a strong or weak single currency.

That such a debate has surfaced at this late stage has suprised many and some worry it has the potential to derail the longstanding alliance between Germany and France on the need for a robust common currency.
French monetary officials also cast doubt on the benefits of linking the French franc to the German mark, a policy that has resulted in low inflation.

Analysts say unless the domestic row spills over into a high profile debate between senior policy-makers in France and Germany, financial markets are likely to remain sanguine about the EMU timetable.

Any hint to the contrary, however, could prompt a flight out of the financial assets of countries on the periphery of Europe and lead to a strengthening of the German mark against most European currencies.
